item.title: More Than 1 in 5 Middle-Income Renters Missed a Full Rent Payment Last Year, New Urban Institute Report Finds
item.body:
For years, the conversation about rent hardship in America focused mostly on lower-income households. A new report from the Urban Institute suggests the pressure is now reaching much further up the income ladder. According to the organization's latest survey data, roughly 22% of middle-income renters said that at some point in 2025 they could not pay their full rent when it was due.

That is a sharp change from the year before, and it is a bigger jump than the one seen among lower-income renters. Here is what the findings say, who is affected, and why researchers are paying close attention.

## The Key Numbers

The findings come from the Urban Institute's Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, which asked more than 10,000 adults about how they are managing everyday costs. The share of renters who said they were unable to pay the full amount of rent at least once in the year breaks down as follows:

| Renter group | Earlier figure | 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Middle-income | about 14% (prior year) | about 22% |
| Lower-income | about 24% (2019) | about 28% |
| Higher-earning | about 5% (prior year) | about 7% |

Two things stand out. First, middle-income renters saw a rise of roughly eight percentage points in a single year. Second, the increase for lower-income renters, while real, has been much more gradual: from about 24% in 2019 to about 28% in 2025. Lower-income renters still report the highest overall rates of trouble paying rent, but the gap between the two groups is narrowing.

## Who Counts as "Middle-Income"?

The report defines middle-income adults by household size. For a single person, that means earning roughly $31,300 to $62,600 a year. For a family of three, the range is roughly $53,300 to $106,600.

Households in these ranges often earn too much to qualify for many housing assistance programs, yet not enough to absorb a sudden jump in rent, a rise in utility bills, or an unexpected expense. That makes them especially exposed when several costs climb at once.

## What "Unable to Pay" Means

In the survey, a renter counts as unable to pay if they could not cover the full amount of rent when it was due. That covers a range of situations, including a late payment, a partial payment, or a missed payment. Not every case ends in a formal eviction filing, and many households catch up later. Still, researchers treat these moments as an early warning sign.

Samantha Batko, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute and a co-author of the report, described the change this way: "This increase among middle-income renters is a big and important shift that reflects overall challenges with affordability in the country." She also noted that when a family reports a late, partial, or missed rent payment, those are choices happening in real time as households try to stretch their budgets.

## A Trend Specific to Renters

The report points to a gap between renters and homeowners. Homeowners' ability to afford their mortgage payments has stayed steady over the past seven years. Rent hardship, by contrast, has been climbing since 2022.

Renters also reported strain beyond the rent itself. More than 20% said they had trouble paying for utilities such as gas, oil, or electricity, which suggests that housing costs are only one part of a broader squeeze on household budgets.

The survey also found that the sharpest increases in missed rent payments during 2025 came in the South and the Northeast.

## Why Researchers Are Concerned

The report ties the trend to mounting economic pressures and the rising cost of everyday necessities. When groceries, transportation, insurance, and utilities all cost more, rent is often the largest bill to come up short.

Batko also raised a longer-term concern about the shift toward middle-income households, noting the potential implications for the number of people who could eventually lose their housing. Households with more income often have more options, such as savings, credit, or help from family, and researchers watch closely for the point where those cushions run out.

## A Note on the Numbers

Reports of this kind rely on self-reported survey responses, so the figures are best read as estimates of how many renters say they struggled, not a count of court filings or formal evictions. Some news coverage has summarized the middle-income finding as "one in five," while the underlying data put it slightly higher, at about 22%. The direction of the trend is clear either way.

## What Renters Can Do

Housing costs are not something any one household can fix alone, but a few practical steps can help anyone who expects to fall behind:

- **Communicate early.** Landlords and property managers are often more willing to discuss a payment plan before a payment is missed than after.
- **Know your local options.** Many cities and counties run emergency rental assistance or mediation programs. Dialing 211 in most areas connects callers to local support services.
- **Seek free housing counseling.** HUD-approved housing counseling agencies offer free or low-cost guidance. A directory is available at hud.gov.
- **Review the lease.** Understanding late-fee rules and notice requirements in your state can help you plan.

## The Bottom Line

The Urban Institute's findings add to a growing body of evidence that housing affordability is no longer only a low-income issue. With about 22% of middle-income renters reporting a missed or incomplete rent payment last year, the strain now reaches households that were once considered financially secure. Whether the trend continues will depend on rents, wages, and the cost of other basics in the months ahead.

*Source: Urban Institute Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, as reported by [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/23/nx-s1-5977022/rent-affordability-middle-income) on September 23, 2026. This article is for general information only and does not constitute financial or legal advice.*
